page_title: Microservices aren't the problem. Incompetent people are

sources.entry: Microservices aren't the problem. Incompetent people are

summary.title: Microservices aren't the problem. Incompetent people are
summary.one_liner: Organisational incompetence and lack of ownership, not microservices themselves, are what make systems hard to work on, and SOLID principles can be applied at system and team levels to help.
takeaways: Microservices are not inherently the problem; poor engineering competence and lack of ownership cause complex, hard-to-maintain systems.
SOLID principles (single responsibility, open-closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion) can be applied to code, systems and organisations alike.
Clear team ownership of services improves motivation, knowledge retention, estimation and code quality, whereas shared ownership leads to neglect.
Adopting new technology without training or handholding makes experienced engineers effectively junior; example given is Kafka being used as a message queue.
Keep designs simple, avoid overcomplicating, and speak up about problems rather than accepting the status quo.
summary.summary: The author argues that microservices are not the real problem; the real problems are lack of engineering competence, hype-driven adoption of new technology without proper learning, and a "not giving a shit" culture. The essay applies SOLID principles at code, system and organisational levels, and compares monolith and service-oriented code via a short example of direct calls versus API calls. It then covers the costs of shared code ownership, developer experience, KISS, avoiding all-or-nothing migrations, and governance, ending with advice to take ownership and speak up. It is an opinion essay with informal, profane language and few formal benchmarks.
